item.content:encoded:
Walk the halls of KubeCon + CloudNativeCon North America 2026 in Salt Lake City, and you’ll notice a subtle but unmistakable shift in how engineers talk about AI. A year ago, the dominant question was whether Kubernetes could handle AI workloads at all. This year, nobody is debating capability anymore. Instead they’re wrestling with the messy reality of running AI in production.

The conversations in Salt Lake City kept circling back to a single tension: enterprises want the speed of autonomous AI, but they aren’t willing to burn down their existing security, governance, and operational models to get it. Here is where the cloud-native ecosystem is actually heading.

AI Infrastructure Is Growing Up and Moving Into the Core

If there was any doubt that AI has become central to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation’s (CNCF) roadmap, the numbers settled it. In its 2026 ecosystem milestones announcement, CNCF reported that its portfolio has reached 231 hosted projects, with 32 added over the past year alone.

What stands out isn’t just the volume of new projects, though, but it’s what they’re trying to solve. With newcomers like Agent Substrate, OpenShell, and OpenRL, alongside llm-d 1.0 and HAMi’s move into incubation, the community is shifting from “how do we schedule a GPU?” to “how do we manage inference routing, accelerator sharing, and agent execution at scale?”

The real bottleneck for enterprises now isn’t a lack of tooling; it’s integration. Nobody wants to maintain a bespoke, disconnected infrastructure stack just to serve models. The winning pattern emerging from KubeCon is embedding GPU scheduling, isolation, and observability directly into the same Kubernetes control plane teams already trust.

Platform Engineering Has a New User…and It Isn’t Human

Platform engineering has officially gone mainstream. According to CNCF’s State of Cloud Native Development Q3 2026 report, 93% of developers now work inside organizations using some form of DevOps standardization or internal developer platform, up from 77% just a year ago.

Just as platform teams figured out how to build great self-service portals for human developers, however, a completely different kind of consumer showed up: autonomous AI agents.

Agents don’t click through dashboards or read internal wikis. They hit APIs directly, chain tools together, and trigger operational changes across systems in milliseconds. Trying to govern an autonomous agent with workflows designed for humans is a recipe for trouble. Projects like OpenShell and the broader push around agent identity point to where platform engineering has to go next while treating agents as first-class workloads by solving three core governance questions:

  1. Identity and Authorization: How are agent credentials managed and strictly scoped?
  2. Delegation: How is authority safely passed across distributed services without over-privileging the agent?
  3. Auditability: How are autonomous actions observed and logged in real time?

Conformance Needs to Move Up the Stack

As Kubernetes stretches to absorb AI, virtualization, and edge workloads, portability is once again front and center. Passing baseline Kubernetes conformance tells you a cluster meets the spec, but it doesn’t guarantee your workload won’t break when you move it between environments.

That’s why two complementary milestones at KubeCon matter so much. First, the Kubernetes AI Conformance Program hit 40 certified platforms, giving teams a reliable baseline for AI-ready infrastructure. VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service (VKS) is among the platforms certified under the program, providing enterprises with a conformant Kubernetes runtime integrated into VMware Cloud Foundation. With support for GPU-enabled workloads, automated cluster lifecycle management, and enterprise security controls, VKS provides a foundation for running AI applications and emerging agentic workloads, including those built using technologies such as Agent Substrate. 

Second, the emerging Kubernetes Workload Conformance Working Group is tackling the harder half of the problem: ensuring that security, networking, storage, and resource behavior stay predictable for the application itself across different clusters.

Conformance is only part of the equation. Enterprises also need flexibility in choosing the tools that support their applications. Broadcom’s expanding VKS ISV partner ecosystem brings validated solutions across security, observability, networking, storage, and AI, helping organizations build production-ready Kubernetes environments without being limited to a single vendor’s tooling.

Preserving that kind of architectural choice is also what drives Broadcom’s upstream work. The VM API project, newly accepted into the CNCF Sandbox, is developing a provider-neutral Kubernetes API for virtual machine lifecycle management, enabling teams to manage VMs using the same declarative workflows they use for containers without tying the API to a single infrastructure provider. 

KubeVM Service brings this approach to VMware Cloud Foundation, allowing teams to provision and manage native vSphere VMs through Kubernetes and GitOps while retaining existing virtualization capabilities, operational visibility, and governance. For a closer look at how these technologies work together, see How VM API and KubeVM Service Deliver Open Standards and Enterprise Execution. You can also read more about how we’re approaching VM and workload portability in Advancing the Cloud-Native Ecosystem Through Open Collaboration.

Operational Resilience and Open-Source Sustainability

It’s easy to get distracted by shiny new agent frameworks at KubeCon, but stateful AI pipelines still live and die by unglamorous fundamentals like storage and disaster recovery. Upstream progress on Velero 1.19 which brings block-level incremental backup and restore and the Container Object Storage Interface (COSI) reflects a simple truth: you can’t claim production readiness for AI if you can’t reliably back up, move, and recover the data feeding it.

Just as important is the human capacity behind the code. The global cloud-native developer population reached 21.2 million in 2026. While AI-assisted coding is making it easier than ever to open a pull request, flooding open-source repositories with generated code puts massive strain on maintainers. Watching CNCF recognize mentors and documentation leaders at the 2026 Community Awards was a timely reminder that sustainable governance and human review (not just code velocity) are what keep this ecosystem resilient.

Looking Toward 2027

If KubeCon NA 2026 proved anything, it’s that the experimentation phase is over. Enterprises don’t need another standalone AI tool. What they do need are unified platforms, predictable workload portability, and battle-tested operational controls.

At Broadcom, our focus across upstream projects like VM API, Velero, COSI, and workload conformance comes down to helping teams bridge that gap without sacrificing openness. (For a full recap of our technical sessions and demos from the show floor, check out AI, Kubernetes, and Cloud Native Innovations: Broadcom at KubeCon North America 2026.) 

Heading into 2027, the real winners in cloud native won’t be the teams running the most experiments; they’ll be the ones who figured out how to make those experiments boring, repeatable, and safe in production.

item.content:encoded:
Server memory prices have surged over the past year, with some DRAM modules rising as much as 60% in a single month and no meaningful relief until 20271 and prices for server vendors are under even more pressure as lead times stretch from weeks to months2. Glencore, one of the world’s largest diversified natural resource companies, responded by deploying NVMe memory tiering, a standard capability in VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF), across its global infrastructure. The feature pairs DRAM with high-capacity NVMe solid-state drives in a single memory pool, and it has already doubled available memory in key Glencore environments without a matching rise in DRAM spend. It’s running in production today, and the business case gets stronger every time memory prices climb.

A global operation feeling the squeeze

Glencore produces and markets more than 60 commodities across 70 vCenters and roughly 50 locations worldwide. When a server procurement quote more than tripled in price in a matter of months, the infrastructure team got direct confirmation that DRAM-only provisioning was becoming financially untenable. A metro cluster resilience requirement at the Baar, Switzerland headquarters compounded the problem by capping usable DRAM at 50% of any host’s capacity (see the full case study for the metro cluster details).

How NVMe memory tiering works

VCF combines fast DRAM (Tier 0) with NVMe solid-state drives (Tier 1) into one memory pool, keeping hot data on DRAM and shifting cold data to NVMe automatically. A 1.6-terabyte NVMe drive costs roughly what 64 gigabytes of DRAM costs, so Glencore’s standard 1:1 DRAM-to-NVMe configuration doubles total memory for a fraction of the price. Broadcom’s own VCF 9.0 performance testing backs this up: a performance cost below 10% across enterprise benchmarks, up to double virtual machine density, and total cost of ownership savings of up to 40%. The full case study walks through Glencore’s own cost math in more depth.

From careful test to standard practice

Figure 1: Glencore mining operations

Glencore didn’t rush this. The team tested memory tiering on vSphere 8 first, then moved to the latest VCF release, where it became a single cluster configuration setting instead of a manual process. A multi-site evaluation spanning Brisbane, Sydney, and Baar preceded production, and the team retired its test environments once VCF 9.1 early access became available. The result: every new Cisco UCS server Glencore deploys now ships with an NVMe card built in. The case study covers the evaluation path step by step.

Results: more memory, lower costs, no developer complaints

Today, 50% of Glencore’s Linux developer VDI systems run on VCF NVMe memory tiering in production, with roughly 5% of all workloads in the Baar cluster using it so far, an early-stage number, not a ceiling. Standard VDI builds reserve 48 to 96 gigabytes of RAM per desktop even though utilization typically runs 10% to 15%, which is exactly the gap NVMe tiering closes without the matching DRAM outlay. Glencore is now extending the capability beyond VDI into business applications and databases. See the full case study for the complete workload breakdown.

Why this matters for infrastructure budgets right now

This isn’t a one-year pricing blip. TrendForce and Counterpoint Research both expect DRAM contract prices to climb 80-95% quarter-over-quarter into 2026 as AI data center demand keeps competing with enterprise IT for the same memory supply. Glencore’s approach, a disciplined evaluation, a staged rollout, and a hardware standard that compounds savings with every refresh, offers a template for any infrastructure team watching memory eat a growing share of its budget.

  • VMware vSphere
  • VMware Cloud Foundation

  2. iFeelTech. “Why RAM prices are going up in 2026 (and what it means for Business Computers and Servers””, July 9, 2026

item.content:encoded:
The use of extra hardware has been a common element in migrations and upgrades. Extra servers would be provisioned as a new vSphere or vSAN cluster, and workloads would be moved over using vMotion and storage vMotion. It was the de facto approach for migrating from vSAN OSA to vSAN ESA, since no classic in-place migration between the two architectures exist.

But the pricing and availability of hardware in the data center has demanded a more prudent approach. Customers have shared with us that they clearly understand the benefit that vSAN ESA delivers, but are now looking for a leaner, minimalist path to transition their workloads and data to ESA. New capabilities within vSAN now make migrations from OSA to ESA easier and more cost efficient!

A Classic Swing Migration

Our telemetry data shows a large percentage of VMware customers running vSphere or vSAN OSA have servers that fully support vSAN ESA. Many of these servers running OSA already use NVMe storage devices in place—one of the primary requirements for ESA. Other servers often have the appropriate NVMe backplane, and just need NVMe storage devices to be ready for ESA.

The primary migration method used in the scenario described above was a classic swing migration. As shown in “Scenario 2 > Migration Option 2” in the post “Migrating to the Express Storage Architecture in vSAN,” three to six extra hosts were used to create a new cluster followed by a vMotion and storage vMotion migration of the workloads off of the old cluster to the new cluster. When sufficient resources were free on the old cluster, the remaining hosts would be decommissioned and reprovisioned as hosts in the new vSAN ESA cluster.

Figure 1. Classic swing migration from vSAN OSA to ESA

While this strategy is very simple, some found its inherent limitations difficult to overcome, including:

  • A lack of extra swing hosts to perform this migration. The cost and availability of hardware has meant that for many customers, there are no eligible extra hosts available for this task.
  • Insufficient swing hosts to maintain required levels of resilience. Some organizations have a strict requirement on higher levels of resilience, which means they must start with a cluster of six hosts instead of just three.
  • Insufficient rack space and network uplinks to accommodate swing hosts. Rack space and network uplinks can also be at a premium, especially when trying to place hosts in the appropriate leaf of a spine-leaf network.
  • Logistics of moving VM instances and data at the same time. This type of migration previously required the VM instance and the storage must be migrated at the same time. This could be a heavy lift depending on the circumstances.

A New Decoupled Swing Migration

vSAN in VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.1 introduced more flexibility with mounting remote datastores, where vSAN OSA clusters can mount the datastore of vSAN ESA clusters, and vice versa. One can use this capability to perform a decoupled swing migration, where workloads can be migrated from one cluster to another with minimal spare resources. Depending on the circumstances, this decoupled swing migration requires no extra hardware using swing hosts, and is very close in principle to an in-place upgrade of a cluster from OSA to ESA.

Not only will this migration method allow you to potentially avoid the use of swing hosts, but it will also maintain full data resilience of your workloads. Traditional swing migrations were more susceptible to temporary degradations in resilience as cluster host counts changed.

What the Workflow Looks Like

In this example, we will use a vSAN OSA cluster consisting of 20 hosts, with a high amount of CPU utilization, and ~40% storage capacity used. The hosts are fully compatible with ESA, but are running vSAN OSA. This particular example will not use any extra hardware as swing hosts, and have a maximum of only one host’s worth of compute resources offline (N-1) at any given time.

  1. Enter one host into maintenance mode, remove any disk claiming for that host, and remove it from the OSA cluster.
  2. Create a new vSAN ESA cluster, and move this “host 1” into a new vSAN ESA cluster. For the first eight hosts, do not claim any of the disks in yet, as it will only be providing compute resources initially.
  3. Mount the OSA cluster’s datastore to the new vSAN ESA cluster using the datastore sharing feature in 9.1.
  4. Perform a vMotion (compute only) of running VMs onto this first host. This allows the data to remain fully resilient on the new cluster as it is initially being provisioned.
  5. Repeat the process above, one host at a time, until 8 hosts have been moved to the new vSAN ESA cluster. At this point, the OSA cluster will be consuming about 67% of the available cluster capacity.
  6. Claim all of the appropriate storage devices for the hosts in the 8-host vSAN ESA cluster. Auto-RAID in vSAN for VCF 9.1 will automatically set the highest level of data resilience for you. Mount the ESA cluster’s datastore to the vSAN OSA cluster using the datastore sharing feature in 9.1.
  7. From the ESA cluster, perform a storage vMotion of all VM objects from the OSA cluster to the ESA cluster.
  8. For the ninth host in the OSA cluster, enter the host into maintenance mode, remove any disk claiming for that host, and remove it from the OSA cluster. Add this host to the new ESA cluster and claim the appropriate storage devices.
  9. Perform a vMotion (compute only) of one host’s worth of VM workloads.
  10. Repeat steps 8 and 9, until all of the remaining hosts in the OSA cluster have been migrated to the ESA cluster.
  11. Enable the Automatic Rebalance capability in the new vSAN ESA cluster.

Figure 2. Decoupled swing migration from vSAN OSA to ESA without using extra hardware (video)

In this particular scenario, there was never more than one host’s worth of compute capacity offline at any point. The initial 20-host OSA cluster required a substantial amount of free capacity because the cluster capacity decreased significantly during the initial 8-host cluster provisioning process, as shown in step 5, above. The initial capacity utilization, the overall cluster host count, and other variables will impact what is possible using this type of migration that does not use any extra swing hosts.

Who Can Benefit

A decoupled swing migration of workloads to a new vSAN ESA cluster using existing hardware is ideal for customers who:

  • Currently have vSAN OSA clusters using server hardware compatible with vSAN ESA.
  • Currently have vSAN OSA clusters with high workload CPU utilization, but relatively low storage capacity utilization.
  • Currently have little to no extra server hardware or rack space to help with migration from vSAN OSA to ESA.
  • Prefer to decouple the migration of VM instances (via vMotion) from VM storage (via storage vMotion).
  • Must maintain the prescribed levels of resilience during the migration.

Requirements and Caveats

While this more granular method of migration can minimize the need for spare hardware resources, it can introduce additional steps and other considerations, including, but not limited to:

  • Cluster host count. This decoupled swing migration is ideal for larger cluster sizes similar to the example shown above. Larger cluster host counts help keep the percentage of resources absent to a minimum while the migration process takes place.
  • Storage capacity utilization in cluster. A decoupled swing migration requires sufficient free storage capacity on the cluster. This is because several hosts that contribute storage capacity must first be removed from the cluster.
  • vSAN version. This decoupled swing migration uses a feature introduced in vSAN for VCF 9.1.
  • Hardware. The server hardware must be compatible with vSAN ESA. For some environments where the hardware is not already compatible, this may be as little as replacing the storage devices to NVMe storage devices during the decoupled swing migration.

Much like the traditional swing migration, the decoupled swing migration does not apply to first class disks (CNS persistent volumes for Kubernetes), vSAN file services shares, and vSAN iSCSI volumes. This data will need to be migrated independent from this migration prior to the OSA cluster being retired. The vSAN Performance Service on the OSA cluster must also be turned off before the OSA cluster can be fully decommissioned.

Recommendation: On the new ESA cluster, do not enable the “Automatic Rebalance” service until the migration has been completed. This will minimize any unnecessary rebalancing until after the migration procedure is complete.

Let’s Hear from You!

The vSAN Product Team is interested if streamlining this process would be useful for your environment. Please take this brief survey to help us better understand your specific environment, and how we can help you accomplish these types of OSA-to-ESA migrations easier.

Summary

There is a good chance that your server hardware running vSAN OSA can run vSAN ESA as well. Thanks to new capabilities in vSAN for VCF 9.1, a decoupled swing migration can make this transition easier and more cost-efficient than ever before. For more information on migrating to vSAN, see the vSAN Migration Guide.

The VCF 9.1 VPC Networking Mental Model

5VCF 9.1 VPC Networking, Part 5: Four Gates for VPC TrafficComing soon
6VCF 9.1 VPC Networking, Part 6: The VPC North-South Firewall and Its CoverageComing soon

This is Part 2 of the series The VCF 9.1 VPC Networking Mental Model. Part 1 gave the build order. This part explains what each object does and how they relate.

VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.1 puts a cloud-style Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) model on top of NSX. Each object is simple on its own. The value is in seeing how they fit: IP blocks provide addresses, External Connections provide paths, Transit Gateways provide shared routing, Connectivity Profiles bind that routing model to VPCs, and subnet access modes decide how far a workload can talk.

Core idea

An IP block answers “which addresses may I use?” An External Connection answers “which external path may traffic use?” A Transit Gateway answers “how do several VPCs share routing?” A Connectivity Profile carries that Transit Gateway design into a VPC. The subnet access mode answers “how visible should this workload network be?”

In everyday terms, think of an office phone system. Private subnets are internal extensions. Anyone in the building can dial 4021, but nobody outside can. Public subnets are direct-dial numbers listed in the phone book. NAT is the switchboard that places your outside call from the main number, so the person you ring sees the company number, not your extension. The IP blocks are the number ranges the company owns for each kind of line.

1. Start with visibility, not with NAT

Before you pick a subnet type, decide how far its routes must be visible.

This routing scope is the basic design decision. NAT is an extra translation service. It is not a substitute for knowing where routes exist.

2. Why are there several IP blocks?

VCF separates address ownership by the routing scope each block serves.

External IP blocks

An External IP block supplies the addresses that give outside connectivity to VPC workloads. The docs list three uses:

  • Public subnets
  • External IPs
  • Translated IPs for the system-created and user-defined NAT rules, including default outbound NAT

External means outside the VPC, not necessarily the Internet. In the same way, a Public subnet means reachable from the outside data centre network, not necessarily exposed to the Internet.

Two rules apply. External IP blocks must not overlap each other within a project or on the same Tier-0 gateway. They should not overlap with any other CIDR in use.

Private TGW IP blocks

A Private TGW block creates Private-TGW subnets. These addresses are for inter-VPC communication through the Transit Gateway. The usual example is application VPCs reaching DNS, Active Directory, or monitoring in a shared services VPC.

By default the Transit Gateway does not advertise them to the outside data centre. On a centralized connection the provider can turn on Advertised Private IP Blocks. You must then also add the TGW_PRIVATE route advertisement rule to the Transit Gateway attachment before the blocks are advertised.

Private VPC CIDR

The Private VPC CIDR is set on the VPC itself. It supplies addresses to Private-VPC subnets. A Private-VPC subnet is reachable only from inside its VPC.

Private VPC CIDRs may overlap between VPCs. That is useful for repeatable application blueprints and labs. Traffic from these subnets that leaves the VPC goes through NAT.

Provider Outbound SNAT IP block

This block belongs to a provider setting on a centralized connection, Provider Outbound SNAT. It works like this:

  • With the toggle on, the provider controls outgoing traffic, whatever the subnet type.
  • The SNAT IP Block holds the ranges or CIDRs used as the translated IP. It must also be listed in Authorize External IP Blocks.
  • With the toggle on, Authorize External IP Blocks becomes mandatory. Only the blocks listed there are advertised.
  • Any other NAT rule on a Transit Gateway uplink has a higher priority than the provider outbound SNAT rule.

3. What does an External Connection define?

An External Connection is the path from a Transit Gateway to the outside network. The provider shares it with a project. The project attaches it to a Transit Gateway.

Connection type

  • A Centralized connection links the Transit Gateway through a Tier-0 gateway on NSX Edge nodes, which provides the link to the physical fabric. You deploy the Edge nodes and manage their lifecycle. The Transit Gateway has its own HA mode.
  • A Distributed VLAN connection gives lightweight connectivity to the data centre fabric with no NSX Edge nodes and no dynamic routing. Stateful services use Virtual Network Appliances (VNAs).
  • A Distributed VXLAN connection is listed for 9.1.1 and later. It needs EVPN Route Controller nodes and a standards-based EVPN-VXLAN fabric.

A Transit Gateway can have more than one External Connection, for example to separate Internet and intranet paths. All of them must be the same type: all centralized or all distributed. A VPC connects to only one Transit Gateway.

Inbound Remote Networks

A centralized connection has an advanced setting called Inbound Remote Networks. These are the destination networks that VPCs reach through that connection. When a Transit Gateway has several connections, the default route can sit on only one of them. Every other connection needs inbound remote networks to carry traffic.

For example:

  • 10.100.0.0/16 behind the Corporate-DC connection.
  • The default route, 0.0.0.0/0, behind the Internet-Egress connection.

Inbound remote networks must be unique per connection. ECMP networks are not supported. If none is set, the default route is used. They answer “which destinations use this connection?” They are not address pools for VMs.

Authorize External IP Blocks and Advertised Private IP Blocks

The other direction is what the connection advertises:

  • Authorize External IP Blocks sets which external IP blocks the connection may advertise. Left empty, all external IP blocks are advertised. Traffic from these blocks is routed to the external network without NAT.
  • Advertised Private IP Blocks is a toggle that also advertises the Private TGW IP blocks, together with the TGW_PRIVATE route advertisement rule.

Keep the two directions apart. Inbound Remote Networks are destinations outside VCF that VPCs reach through this connection. Authorized and advertised blocks are local VCF prefixes the outside network learns, so it can route back to them.

4. Why must resources be shared with a project?

The Default project can use external connections, external IP blocks and Edge nodes without defining them as shared resources. A user-defined project cannot. You have to share those resources with it.

So the Enterprise Admin shares the External Connections and External IP blocks a project may use. The Project Admin builds Transit Gateways and VPCs from them. This is the boundary between provider governance and tenant self-service.

One limit showed up in the lab. A centralized connection that a Transit Gateway in one project already uses cannot be shared with a second project. The share fails with “TGW external connection … already used in another project” (error 500157). Plan one centralized connection per project, or check the Broadcom docs for the supported sharing options.

5. Transit Gateway: the shared routing hub

The Transit Gateway provides inter-VPC communication and the connection to the outside network through External Connections. Its southbound side connects to VPC Gateways. Its northbound side connects to the External Connections attached to it.

The connection choices are:

  • None: the Transit Gateway has no external connection.
  • Centralized: northbound traffic uses a Tier-0 gateway on NSX Edge nodes.
  • Distributed VLAN: northbound connectivity from the hosts to a VLAN.
  • Distributed VXLAN: northbound connectivity into an EVPN-VXLAN fabric (9.1.1 and later).

Two VPCs on the same Transit Gateway can reach each other’s Private-TGW subnets through it. Private-VPC subnets stay inside their own VPC.

Private-TGW route advertisement

Keep two scopes clear:

  • A Private-TGW subnet is available for inter-VPC communication on its Transit Gateway.
  • Advertising it to the outside network is off by default. It needs the Advertised Private IP Blocks toggle on the connection and the TGW_PRIVATE route advertisement rule.

Only turn on external advertisement when the outside network has a return path and the wider visibility matches the security design.

6. The VPC Connectivity Profile is the contract

A VPC Connectivity Profile ties a VPC to a Transit Gateway. It carries the External IP Blocks and Private TGW IP Blocks the VPC can use, and switches such as N-S Services and Default Outbound NAT. When you create a Transit Gateway, NSX creates a default connectivity profile for it. In the lab it did this for a distributed Transit Gateway as well as a centralized one.

Each VPC uses one Connectivity Profile. Many VPCs can share the same profile. To move a VPC to another Transit Gateway, change its connectivity profile.

Public and Private-TGW subnets in the VPC take their addresses from the blocks in that profile.

7. What is configured on the VPC?

The VPC is the tenant’s logical application boundary. At creation time the important inputs are:

  • The Private VPC CIDR used by Private-VPC subnets.
  • The VPC Connectivity Profile linking the VPC to the Transit Gateway.
  • The VPC Service Profile, which holds DHCP server or relay settings and subnet profiles.
  • Optional VPC static routes.
  • The Enable for Avi Load Balancer toggle. It lets the Avi Load Balancer Controller discover the VPC and needs at least one private IP block and one edge cluster assigned to the VPC.

The VPC Gateway routes between the subnets inside the VPC and northbound toward the Transit Gateway. It is also the default gateway for every subnet. NSX gives each subnet a gateway address, the first usable address in its CIDR, and that address lives on the VPC Gateway. In the lab the Public subnet 10.50.0.64/28 gets 10.50.0.65, and the Private-VPC subnet 172.16.0.0/26 gets 172.16.0.1.

8. The three subnet access modes

Private VPC

Use Private VPC for workloads that should be reachable only from inside one VPC.

  • Address source: the VPC’s Private VPC CIDR
  • Reachable from: inside the same VPC only
  • Private VPC CIDRs can overlap between VPCs
  • Typical use: back-end tiers such as database and application servers
  • Outside access: through NAT

Private TGW

Use Private TGW when workloads in different VPCs must talk through the same Transit Gateway.

  • Address source: the Private TGW IP block
  • Reachable from: VPCs on the same Transit Gateway
  • Typical use: shared services such as DNS, Active Directory and monitoring
  • Outside access: through NAT, or by advertising the Private TGW block (Advertised Private IP Blocks plus the TGW_PRIVATE rule)

Public

Use Public when the subnet must be reachable from outside the VPC.

  • Address source: an External IP block
  • Reachable from: inside the VPC and from the outside data centre network
  • NAT: not needed for this reachability
  • Typical use: front-end web servers that users or management reach directly from the corporate network

Public does not remove the need for firewall policy. Route visibility and security authorization are different controls.

9. NAT: what problem does it solve?

NAT changes the source or destination address at a routing boundary. In this design it does three jobs:

  • Give private subnets outbound access outside the VPC.
  • Map a single private workload to an External IP, instead of making its whole subnet Public.
  • Let the provider control outgoing traffic with provider outbound SNAT.

Default Outbound NAT

Default Outbound NAT is a toggle in the VPC Connectivity Profile. You can also set it when you create a Transit Gateway. It gives workloads on private subnets outbound access outside the VPC. One SNAT rule per VPC is created automatically. The translated IP comes from the profile’s External IP Blocks, or from the block set in External IP Block for Default Outbound NAT.

Because the rule is per VPC, each VPC’s outbound traffic leaves with its own translated address, and the private subnets stay hidden.

External IPs and your own NAT rules

An External IP is a stateless 1:1 NAT for one workload, with the address taken from the External IP block. You can also add your own NAT rules to a VPC. Two limits apply. For SNAT, the source network must not overlap with external IP blocks. For DNAT, the translated network must not overlap with external IP blocks.

Provider Outbound SNAT

Provider outbound SNAT is set on a centralized connection, as described in section 2. It translates outgoing traffic into the provider’s SNAT IP Block, whatever the subnet type. Any other NAT rule on the Transit Gateway uplink has a higher priority.

NAT decision table

You want Use Who sets it
Workloads reachable from outside by their real address A Public subnet, or an authorized Private TGW block Project or VPC admin; provider for advertisement
Private subnets with outbound access Default Outbound NAT in the connectivity profile Project admin
One private workload reachable from outside An External IP VPC admin
All outgoing traffic leaving with provider addresses Provider Outbound SNAT on the connection Provider

10. VLAN extension and access mode

VLAN extension connects a VPC subnet to an existing VLAN. A VLAN-extended subnet uses access mode Public, and DHCP does not apply to it. The form also offers L2 Only once VLAN extension is on, but that mode is for the TEP-less VLAN-backed VPC, where the Transit Gateway has no external connection.

VLAN extension is not another way to connect Private-VPC or Private-TGW routing. It serves a different purpose, which Part 4 will cover in detail.

11. Design checks before production

  • With more than one connection on a Transit Gateway, does only one carry the default route? Do the others have unique inbound remote networks?
  • Are External IP blocks free of overlap within the project, on the Tier-0 gateway and with other CIDRs in use?
  • Are all External Connections on each Transit Gateway the same type?
  • Are Private-TGW prefixes meant to stay inside the Transit Gateway, or be advertised outside?
  • If advertised, are both the toggle and the TGW_PRIVATE rule in place? Does the outside network have a return route?
  • If not advertised, which NAT provides the translated source?
  • If Provider Outbound SNAT is on, is the SNAT IP Block also in Authorize External IP Blocks?
  • Does each VPC use the intended Connectivity Profile?
  • Is VLAN extension needed, or would routed connectivity be simpler?

Once route visibility is clear, the NAT decision is simple. Route the real address when the network should know it. Translate the address when it should not.

What’s next

Part 3, coming soon, opens the hood on the Distributed Transit Gateway: how a VPC reaches the physical network with no NSX Edge and no routing protocol, and the three paths traffic takes out of a VPC.

item.content:encoded:
The layer every other control trusts

5G’s cloud-native decomposition placed the mobile core — control plane (AMF, SMF, NRF, AUSF, UDM, PCF, NEF, NSSF, SEPP) and user plane (UPF, GTP-U on N3/N9, N6, PFCP on N4) — onto virtualized infrastructure, most commonly VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) with ESX hypervisors. 

Every layer of defense for VCF built to date (vDefend microsegmentation, mTLS/OAuth2 at the SBA, confidential computing for memory, EDR for guest workloads, etc.) assumes one thing:  ESX hypervisor is the most important security boundary you own. Every control you have invested in assumes it is trustworthy. 

That assumption in an AI world can be your weakest link. AI-accelerated attack tools discover and weaponize vulnerabilities at machine speed, shrinking the patch window from months to hours, while stolen root credentials remain the single most common route into the hypervisor. Acknowledging the shifting security landscape, Broadcom introduced VMware HyperArmor to make that assumption a reality rather than a hope.

The problems behind most Hypervisor attacks 

Two problems account for most hypervisor attacks: stolen root credentials and unpatched vulnerabilities. Both are directly relevant to telecom 5G:

Stolen root credentials

Communication Service Providers (CSP) operations teams reach ESX hosts over SSH for troubleshooting, patching, and emergency work, often from a central NOC or through jump hosts. A phished or leaked root password gives an attacker the command line of a host that may carry a dozen virtual network functions (NFs) and cloud-native network functions (CNFs).

CVE-2024-37085 showed how this cascades. Attackers who had already compromised Active Directory created an “ESX Admins” group, gained full ESX admin rights, and deployed ransomware against every VM on the host. In a telco cloud, that is an outage measured in subscribers, not servers.

Unpatched vulnerabilities and the collapsing patch window

The patch window is the gap between a vulnerability’s disclosure and a tested patch in production. AI-driven attack tooling now finds and weaponizes obscure flaws faster than IT teams can test fixes.

Telco change control works in the opposite direction. ESX upgrades need network function (NF) vendor regression testing, change-board approval, and a maintenance window on a platform that runs 24/7. The next window may be weeks away while the exploit is available today. Edge sites are usually patched last, so they stay exposed longest.

What does that mean for a Telco?

•      One compromised host exposes every NF on it, whatever the guest-level controls.

•      Ransomware aimed at ESX encrypts all VMs at once, turning a host incident into a service outage.

•      Your exposure time is set by your change calendar, while the attacker’s timeline is set by automation.

What does HyperArmor bring to your telco cloud?

HyperArmor is a software add-on for the ESX hypervisor in VCF as a proactive, real-time defense layer for the ESX component of VCF, and thus applies to your 5G core and edge clusters.

VMware HyperArmor has three pillars:

1. Host-level virtual patching

HyperArmor detects and blocks attempts to exploit a host before the vulnerability can be used, with no host reboot and no software upgrade. It extends the network-layer virtual patching that vDefend already provides down to the hypervisor itself.

For a CSP, this turns the strategy from “exposed until the next maintenance window” to “mitigated now, patched on schedule.”

2. Positive Host Security Guardrails

ESX runs a small, fixed set of processes, which makes it a natural fit for allowlisting. HyperArmor builds a known-good baseline, inventories existing scripts and allows them, and then blocks any unauthorized executable or script. It is agentless, monitors continuously, and adds minimal overhead.

The practical effect, as Heise describes it, is that an exploit may reach a vulnerability but cannot download or plant malicious code.

3. Hypervisor-level MFA

A time-based one-time password (TOTP) challenge sits directly in the ESX SSH login path. It is tied to a separately defined identity, so a stolen root password alone does not reach the command line.

Why does the design fit how CSPs operate?

Most host-security tools fail in telco clouds for operational reasons, not technical ones: they need reboots, agents, or upgrades that collide with certification and change control. HyperArmor’s design constraints line up with those realities.

The result is time. Security teams get a much shorter risk window, and platform teams keep the freedom to test and apply official patches on their own schedule.

Defending the control-plane hosts

Control-plane hosts are where HyperArmor should land first. They carry your most valuable secrets: subscriber credential stores, authentication key material, and the NRF’s OAuth2 token-signing key. A single compromised host here can lead to a subscriber credential breach or network-wide policy manipulation.

The host-layer threats

•      Stolen SSH credentials: With root, an attacker can read VM memory that is not protected by confidential computing, mount virtual disks offline, change VM configuration, and pivot toward vCenter.

•      Unpatched ESX flaws: Every day between disclosure and your maintenance window is exposure and AI tooling shrinks the attacker’s side of that gap to hours.

•      Unauthorized code on the host: Ransomware, cryptominers, reverse shells, and lateral-movement tools all need to run a process or write files on ESX.

•      ESX-targeted ransomware: The most common real-world disaster: every VM on the host is encrypted, taking down every control-plane NF it carries.

How does HyperArmor answer each one?

MFA protects the hosts that hold your credential stores.

With TOTP in the SSH path, a leaked root password cannot reach the shell of the host running AUSF, UDM or the NRF. This breaks the most common chain (stolen credential, host access, key theft) at the front door. Because the second factor uses a separate identity, a compromised AD or vCenter account does not hand over SSH access. That is a direct defense against the CVE-2024-37085 pattern case.

Guardrails enforce a known-good baseline.

An attacker who does reach an NRF host cannot launch a credential-dumping tool. One who reaches an AUSF/UDM host cannot run a memory scraper. Enforcement happens at the infrastructure layer, so vendor-certified NFs from Ericsson, Nokia, Cisco, and others are untouched.

Virtual patching closes the exposure window. 

ESX patching at Telcos can take weeks of change control and NF regression testing. HyperArmor blocks exploitation attempts on the host in the meantime, with no reboot. Paired with vDefend’s virtual patching at the vNIC, you get two interim layers: vDefend stops network-level exploit patterns reaching the NF and HyperArmor stops exploitation of the hypervisor itself.

Ransomware kill chain breaks before encryption starts. 

ESX ransomware has to run unauthorized processes and write encrypted payloads to disk. The guardrails block both, protecting every control-plane NF on the host from the scenario operators fear most.

Control-plane deployment notes

•      Blast radius: These are your highest-value hosts, so deploy here first.

•      Change control: Adding HyperArmor is still a platform change, but no reboots and no guest agents keep the approval light.

•      Baseline governance: Set a formal process for approving new scripts on control-plane hosts, to avoid both false blocks and an allowlist that grows too large.

•      Patch hosts: Virtual patching buys time; it does not replace the official patch.

•      Compliance and auditing: The hypervisor-level MFA and guardrail logs of HyperArmor integrate directly into SIEM pipelines, supporting strict regulatory frameworks like NIST SP 800-53 Rev-5 and 3GPP TS 33.501 for OAM traceability.

Defending user-plane hosts

User-plane hosts carry live subscriber traffic and many of them sit at edge sites with weaker physical security and nobody on site. That combination makes HyperArmor’s agentless, no-reboot model especially valuable at the edge.

The host-layer threats

•      Edge host compromise: Someone with physical or network access to an edge ESX host running a UPF can go after the hypervisor directly.

•      Host-level UPF manipulation: From the host, an attacker can mount the UPF’s virtual disk offline to pull session data, change VM configuration to redirect traffic, or encrypt the UPF and cut service.

•      Escalation beyond protocol attacks: GTP-U floods and crafted packets target the UPF application; owning the host gives an attacker far more power than any of them.

•      Ransomware at the edge: Edge sites are attractive targets precisely because recovery is slow, with remote hands only.

How does HyperArmor answer each one?

MFA secures remote access to edge hosts. 

Edge ESX access is almost always remote, from the NOC or through jump hosts. TOTP in the SSH path means a stolen or brute-forced root password cannot reach the shell. A cell-site cabinet host gets the same protection as a core data center host, with no extra physical security.

Guardrails lock down the edge UPF host. 

At an unstaffed site, nobody will notice a rogue process. HyperArmor blocks any unauthorized executable or script, whether the attacker arrived over SSH, through a compromised management network or at the physical console. They cannot run tools to tamper with the UPF VM, extract data from its disks, or launch ransomware. The no-agent design matters doubly here: UPF dataplanes cannot absorb a guest-agent tax and CNF vendor certification would rule one out anyway.

Virtual patching covers your slowest-patched sites. 

Edge sites are usually last in an ESX rollout because of logistics and change windows. HyperArmor protects them against known exploitation techniques now, while the official patch follows the normal schedule.

vDefend and HyperArmor complement each other. 

Where UPF traffic crosses the vNIC path and a signature exists, vDefend IDPS provides network-layer virtual patching for GTP-U and protocol exploits. HyperArmor adds the host layer beneath: if an exploit or a malicious process tries to take over the host itself, the guardrails and host-level virtual patching stop it.

User-plane deployment notes

•      Performance: Performance overhead is minimal but validation with specific NF vendors is . .

•      Scale: Thousands of edge hosts need automated baseline management and central policy administration.

•      Business case: Broadcom pitches HyperArmor at higher-risk workloads. Both control and user planes qualify in telecom.

•      Scope: HyperArmor protects the ESX host, not the inside of the UPF VM or CNF. Use vDefend Guest Introspection, CNF runtime security, andUPF-native controls for that, where supported.

Control plane vs. user plane at a glance

The three pillars are the same on every host; what changes is which one matters most and how you run it.

HyperArmor in your defense-in-depth stack

HyperArmor does not replace any control you run today. It protects the layer that all of them depend on.

HyperArmor prevents at the host, ESX EDR detects at the host, vDefend covers the network, mTLS and OAuth2 cover the service-based interfaces, and confidential computing covers memory. An attacker who slips past one layer may still be stopped or seen by another, but that might not be enough sometimes so host hardening, management-plane monitoring, identity controls, and tested recovery remain mandatory.

One important point to remember is that vDefend rules are enforced by the hypervisor, mTLS terminates in VMs or the hypervisor hosts, and confidential VMs still depend on the ESX host for lifecycle and availability. HyperArmor is the layer that protects the layer everything else relies on.

Conclusion

HyperArmor turns the hypervisor under your 5G core and edge from an assumed-trust layer into an enforced trust boundary. It tackles the two problems behind most hypervisor attacks: stolen root credentials through SSH MFA and unpatched flaws through host-level virtual patching. Positive guardrails stop unauthorized code even when an attacker reaches the host.

On the control plane, it shields the hosts holding your most sensitive keys and credential stores, where one breach can spread network-wide. On the user plane, it brings strong host protection to edge sites where patching is slowest, physical security is weakest, and on-site response is absent without taxing the dataplane or breaking vendor certification.

Ready to harden your telco infrastructure?

  • Explore more about VMware HyperArmor.
  • Contact your Broadcom account representative for assessment and proof-of-concept.

item.content:encoded:
Series · Part 1 of 6
The VCF 9.1 VPC Networking Mental Model
1VCF 9.1 VPC Networking, Part 1: From External Connection to VPCYou are here
2VCF 9.1 VPC Networking, Part 2: IP Blocks, External Connections, Transit Gateways, Subnets and NATComing soon
3VCF 9.1 VPC Networking, Part 3: The Distributed Transit GatewayComing soon
4VCF 9.1 VPC Networking, Part 4: VLAN Extension Under the HoodComing soon
5VCF 9.1 VPC Networking, Part 5: Four Gates for VPC TrafficComing soon
6VCF 9.1 VPC Networking, Part 6: The VPC North-South Firewall and Its CoverageComing soon

This is Part 1 of the series The VCF 9.1 VPC Networking Mental Model. It covers the order in which a Virtual Private Cloud (VPC) is built, from the provider’s External Connection down to the workload subnets. Later parts go deeper into each object.

VPC networking in VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) 9.1 is easiest to understand as a controlled hand-off. The default project holds the provider-owned constructs: External IP blocks and External Connections. A project is granted access to the ones it needs. Inside that project, a Transit Gateway sets the northbound model, a VPC consumes the matching connectivity and service profiles, and subnets become the networks the workloads sit on.

Core idea

Build the provider-side connectivity first. Delegate it to the project. Then let the project consume the correct transit, connectivity, and service profiles.

In everyday terms, think of a large apartment building. The provider is the building manager. They own the street entrance (the External Connection) and decide which flat numbers exist (the IP blocks). Each project is a tenant who rents a floor and arranges the flats on it (the VPCs) as they like. Tenants never build a new door to the street. They use the entrance the manager gave them.

1. Start in the default project

The default project is where the provider builds reusable external connectivity. Create the External IP Blocks needed for public subnets, External IPs, and NAT-translated addresses. Then define the External Connection that describes how the VPC domain reaches the physical network.

Choose the External Connection type

The External Connection is not just a label. Its type decides the data path and which centralized services are possible.

  • A Centralized Connection links the Transit Gateway through a Tier-0 gateway on NSX Edge nodes. The design guide lists stateful services for this model: Default Outbound NAT, custom NAT, Gateway Firewall, External IPs, load balancing, and VPN.
  • A Distributed VLAN Connection gives lightweight connectivity to the data centre fabric with no NSX Edge nodes and no dynamic routing. Stateful services run on Virtual Network Appliances (VNAs). The design guide also describes a VLAN Backed VPC model, introduced in 9.1.1, for TEP-less designs. Part 4 covers it.
  • A Distributed VXLAN Connection integrates with a standards-based EVPN-VXLAN fabric. The design guide lists it for 9.1.1. It needs EVPN Route Controller nodes to exchange BGP EVPN routes, and VNAs for stateful services.

2. Delegate provider constructs to the project

Projects give administrative and configuration isolation. Before a project administrator can build a VPC, the provider must grant the project access to the right External Connection and External IP Blocks. This delegation is the control point. It stops a project from consuming arbitrary provider networks or address space.

Note

Architecture check. A Transit Gateway can have several External Connections, but they must all be the same type: all centralized or all distributed. A VPC connects to only one Transit Gateway.

3. Create the project Transit Gateway

Move into the target project. Create the Transit Gateway from Networking, VPC Connectivity, Transit Gateways. Select the External Connection shared in the previous step. The Transit Gateway provides both inter-VPC communication and the connection to the outside network.

  • Select the delegated External Connection.
  • Enter the VPC External IP Blocks the gateway design needs.
  • Add Private Transit Gateway IP Blocks when private transit addressing is part of the model.
  • Confirm the connection type and the network span before attaching VPCs.
Tip

The project now has a defined path to the external network and the addressing it needs for VPC connectivity. Check that everything shows as realized before you go on.

4. Create the VPC with the matching profiles

In the target project, open the VPCs tab and click Add VPC. Enter the private VPC CIDRs, select the VPC Connectivity Profile, and check the External and Private TGW IP blocks it brings. The profile is the reusable northbound configuration the VPC consumes.

Service profile and Avi integration

A VPC Service Profile holds the DHCP server or relay settings and the subnet profiles. Avi is a separate setting on the VPC. Turn on Enable for Avi Load Balancer so the Avi Load Balancer Controller can discover the VPC. The toggle has two conditions: at least one private IP block and at least one edge cluster assigned to the VPC. The private block is needed because the virtual service IP sits on a private subnet. The edge cluster lets the Service Engines get addresses from the DHCP server.

5. Create workload-facing VPC subnets

Create subnets only after the VPC has the right northbound and service context. Choose the access mode and the address source on purpose. Public subnets take addresses from an External IP block. Private-TGW subnets take them from the Private TGW IP block. Private-VPC subnets take them from the VPC’s private CIDR. VLAN extension uses a Distributed VLAN Connection and is covered in Part 4.

Validation checklist

  • All External Connections and External IP Blocks show successful realization.
  • The project sees only the provider constructs meant for it.
  • The Transit Gateway uses the correct connection type and External Connection.
  • The VPC consumes the intended connectivity and service profiles.
  • External IP blocks do not overlap within the project or on the same Tier-0 gateway. Subnets match their Public, Private or VLAN intent.
  • Routes are present in NSX and in the physical network where advertisement is needed.
  • NAT, firewall and external reachability behave as designed.
  • VPCs with Enable for Avi Load Balancer on have a private IP block and an edge cluster assigned.

Design takeaways

Takeaway Why
Provider first External Connections and External IP Blocks start in the default project and are shared with projects.
Match the model Centralized, Distributed VLAN and Distributed VXLAN are different data-plane designs. All connections on one Transit Gateway must be the same type.
Edges only where required A centralized connection uses a Tier-0 gateway on NSX Edge nodes. A Distributed VLAN connection needs no Edge nodes. Its stateful services run on VNAs.
Profiles carry intent Connectivity and service profiles let many VPCs consume the same northbound and service configuration.

Official references

  • External Connections
  • Transit Gateways
  • Add a VPC Connectivity Profile
  • Add a VPC Service Profile
  • Configure VLAN-backed VPC Subnets in VCF 9.1
  • Add an External Connection for Distributed VXLAN Connectivity

What’s next

Part 2 takes each object from this build order and explains what it does: the IP blocks and why there are several, what an External Connection defines, how the Transit Gateway and the Connectivity Profile fit, the three subnet access modes, and where NAT comes in.

About the co-author

This series is co-written with Abhilash Pillai, an Architect in Broadcom’s VCF Division. Over the past 16 years he has designed and delivered network, security, data centre, and cloud platforms. He holds the CCDE, CCIE Routing and Switching, CCIE Security, CISSP, CCSK, TOGAF and multiple VCF VCAP certifications.

item.content:encoded:
We’re excited to announce the first VMmark benchmark results using new AMD EPYC 9006 Series Server CPUs. Submitted by Dell Technologies across 1-socket PowerEdge R9815 and 2-socket PowerEdge R9825 configurations, these two server platforms set a number of records in both performance and power-performance: see the VMmark Results page for more information.

Here are some of the highlights:

  • The PowerEdge R9815 and R9825 lead the VMmark 1-socket and 2-socket server performance categories, respectively.
  • They also have the top-ranked VMmark Performance-Per-Kilowatt (PPKW) scores in both Server Power-Performance and Server and Storage Power-Performance categories, which were added in VMmark 4.1. For more information, see: Introducing VMmark 4.1: Enhanced Power Efficiency Benchmarking for Private Cloud Infrastructure
  • These systems are powered by new 6th Generation AMD EPYC 9996 “Venice” CPUs featuring 256 cores, 512 threads, and 1024 MB L3 cache.
  • By enabling the latest CPU architectures, Broadcom, through VMware Cloud Foundation, brings each new CPU generation to private cloud infrastructure with scale and efficiency you can measure.

Let’s compare a 5th Generation AMD EPYC “Turin” VMmark result to one on the new 6th Generation AMD EPYC “Venice” platform to see how performance scales across generations:

VCF 9.1.2 enables support for these new CPUs, but performance across 9.1 maintenance releases remains virtually unchanged. The significant score jump is driven entirely by the new hardware generation.

A 60% increase in core count translates directly into a 70% higher VMmark score. By sustaining 5.8 tiles (121 VMs) compared to the R7715’s 3.8 tiles (77 VMs)—where each tile simulates a realistic mix of modern data center workloads—the R9815 drives a 57% increase in workload capacity. For private cloud environments, this means organizations can handle significantly higher compute demand while consolidating onto fewer physical servers during a hardware refresh.

Here are some resources to learn more:

  • VMmark 4
  • VMmark Community
  • VMware Cloud Foundation 9.1
  • Dell PowerEdge R9815, R9825
  • AMD EPYC 9006 Server CPUs

These comparisons are based on all VMmark results published as of 11/10/2026. VMmark is a free benchmarking tool provided as-is by Broadcom and used by partners and customers to measure the performance, scalability, and power consumption of virtualization platforms.

item.content:encoded:
In VMware Cloud Foundation (VCF) Operations 9.1 the Broadcom team has re-engineered the Diagnostics Management Pack. We split the Diagnostics Management Pack into two parts, the Diagnostics Management Pack and the Diagnostics Content Pack, so we can deliver findings more quickly to our customers. 

When the findings were bundled into the Diagnostics Management pack, they were released along with product releases. This limited the number of finding releases and increased the time to inform customers of new security vulnerabilities and known issues in their environments. Splitting the findings out of this management pack allows us to add content packs to the Solution Catalog and not tie finding releases to solely product releases. The best way to think of this is the Anti-Virus definition model: the Diagnostics Management Pack is the required engine component and the Diagnostics Content Pack is the definition file that gives signatures of the known vulnerabilities. A new feature alerts customers when a new content pack is released to the solution catalog. From the Active Findings screen and Findings Catalog, customers will see the following notification banner. 

In the first content pack that we released to both VCF Operations 9.1.0 and 9.1.1, we included security-based, adoption blocking, and high global support trending issues. Most of the proceeding content packs will be focused on VMSA/CVE type findings. Below are some highlights of the findings in this content pack. 

Security Vulnerabilities

In VMSA-2026-0006, Broadcom informs customers of multiple CVEs impacting both vCenter and ESX. VMware vCenter contains an authentication bypass vulnerability in the VMware Directory Service (CVE-2026-59309). A malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this issue to bypass authentication and gain unauthorized access to the system. VMware vCenter contains a directory traversal vulnerability in the Syslog server (CVE-2026-59310). A malicious actor with network access to vCenter may exploit this issue to execute arbitrary code. VMware ESX contains an out-of-bounds write vulnerability in the VMXNET3 virtual network adapter. A malicious actor with local administrative privileges on a virtual machine with VMXNET3 virtual network adapter may exploit this issue to execute code on the host. 

vCenter_CVE_2026_59309to10_VMSA_202606 / ESX_CVE_2026_47876_VMSA_202606

  • https://support.broadcom.com/web/ecx/support-content-notification/-/external/content/SecurityAdvisories/0/38017
  • Critical

VCF Adoption Blocking Issues

Broadcom Technical Support has been focusing on resolving adoption blocking issues. One of the findings found in the content pack is a vCenter UUID case mismatch which impacts vCenter licensing. This is a vCenter Instance UUID case mismatch between vCenter and VCF Operations that causes this issue. This issue is resolved in VMware vCenter 9.1.0.0200. The workaround for this issue is to match the UUID case between VCF Operations and vCenter server. 

vCenter_UUIDCaseMismatch_KB_440982

  • https://knowledge.broadcom.com/external/article/440982
  • Immediate

Broadcom Technical Support Trending Issues

Broadcom Technical Support trending issues are Knowledge Base articles that have solved many cases and/or are viewed many times. One of the findings in the content pack is a vCenter login failure. This can happen when the client credentials used by the vCenter’s oauth2 client becomes invalid because it has expired. In VCF 9.0, there is a logic to rotate the vCenter’s OAuth2 client credentials every 90 days. This issue is resolved in vCenter 9.0.2 and workarounds are available in 9.0.0 and 9.0.1. 

vCenter_oauth2credentialsinvalid_KB_414489

  • https://knowledge.broadcom.com/external/article/414489
  • Immediate

We plan on releasing more Diagnostics Content Packs in the next coming weeks. Please subscribe to KB https://knowledge.broadcom.com/external/article/371661 for the latest updates.
